## The Thursday tea trolley could do with two more of us

After 41 years of bookkeeping, mostly for a builders’ merchant in Dereham, I retired and found that I had no regular reason to go out most weeks. I drifted along like that for about eighteen months. Then, in March 2022, I started volunteering on the Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit at Wensum Vale Hospice.

My first week was not especially promising. I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. A patient called Pat laughed so much that she had to be given a tissue, and told me it was the best afternoon she’d had in a month. I have been going back ever since, though I am now more careful with the milk.

People sometimes imagine that a hospice must be either harrowing to work in or full of people doing terribly skilled things. Thursdays in the day unit are generally neither. There are usually between 14 and 18 patients. Many come for the art group or hand massage, and some simply come for company. Most go home again afterwards. While they are here, we go round with tea, coffee and biscuits, and stop for a chat where one is wanted.

It is often noisy and rather jolly. The bourbon biscuits always disappear first, so we now hide a packet for the late group. Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and insists on telling me about the 1953 floods each week. The story changes slightly every time. I have stopped correcting the dates.

That is not to pretend every week is easy. Some days are sad, and occasionally someone you have become used to seeing is no longer there. When that happens, the staff look after us as well as the patients. You are not left to get on with it alone.

You do not need nursing skills to do this job. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. Forty-one years of keeping ledgers straight turns out to be surprisingly handy for remembering orders, although I never had to hide bourbons in the office.

I would not call it self-sacrifice, either. Thursdays gave my week a fixed point when I badly needed one. I turn up, do something useful, hear several unlikely stories and usually come home having laughed. That seems a fair exchange to me.

At present there are four of us on a rota designed for six. One volunteer moved to Sheffield over the summer to be nearer her grandchildren, and another left to have a knee operation, so we have been two short since then.

The commitment is **one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm**. You will not be sent straight out with a trolley and expected to know what you are doing. Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, provides an induction of about two hours. There is also a short food hygiene course to complete online, which the hospice pays for.

If you are wondering whether it might suit you, the easiest thing is to come to the **volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room**. There will be tea and biscuits, and no obligation to sign up. You can ask questions, meet people and then go home and think about it. Alternatively, ring Bridget on the volunteering line for a chat.

My hope is that at least two people reading this will come along. You need not decide anything on the day. Just come and see what Thursdays are actually like — and ask us where we keep the spare bourbons.
